description: ONE retrieval vocabulary, TWO engine renderings. The single source of truth for what the firehose looks for, shared by the GKG/BigQuery backtest and the Anthropic/Tavily forward gather -- so the backtest stays a valid proxy for the forward (CLAUDE.md: keep the strategy knobs synced across both).
_how_it_is_rendered: query    -> the natural-language beat, run VERBATIM as one web search by forward_gather (Anthropic) and forward_gather_tavily. These strings are FROZEN: the forward paper trade is live and its beats must not drift. Lifted byte-for-byte out of forward_gather.GEM_BEATS / COVERAGE_BEATS.

keywords -> the atoms GKG matches, as a case-insensitive regex alternation against the article's URL (DocumentIdentifier) and page title (Extras). A multi-word atom matches a space, hyphen OR underscore, so 'rare earth' also hits the URL slug 'rare-earth'.
The old src/firehose.GDELT_QUERIES boolean strings are the DOC API's rendering and stay in firehose.py; the DOC API remains the keyless fallback for recent windows.
_atom_specificity_rule: MEASURED 2026-08-07, and the reason this file was rewritten once already. An atom must be a term that essentially ONLY occurs in a market or industry context. Bare sector words do NOT qualify: the first draft used generic atoms and the 56-day pool came back at 320,798 articles, of which the beat 'war chokepoint stock beneficiary' alone claimed 91,053 -- the atom `war` matching every war story on earth, and `energy`/`oil`/`gas` claiming another 59,882. Top source was a radio network. The rule that replaced it: prefer a multi-word compound ('crude oil', 'regional bank', 'tanker rates') over the bare noun ('oil', 'bank', 'shipping'); prefer the industry term over the everyday word. Note this is the OPPOSITE pressure from the natural-language `query` strings, which a semantic engine reads as intent -- a regex reads them literally, which is exactly the mistake the first draft made.
_why_no_vehicle_clause: firehose.GDELT_QUERIES ANDs every sector beat with _VEHICLE = (stock OR ETF OR shares OR equities), because the DOC API is lexical and had no other way to ask 'is this article about a listed company'. Deliberately NOT reproduced as an atom requirement here -- a headline that never says the word 'stock' is exactly the early coverage worth having, and a Boolean AND can only shrink recall. The job is done instead by engine.market_themes (GDELT's own topic classification) AND the subject-org test, both of which are semantic rather than lexical. NOTE: an earlier version of this file claimed the subject-org test ALONE replaced the vehicle clause. It does not -- 'names an organization' is not 'is about a listed company', and without the theme gate the pool filled with general news that happened to name an org.
_origin_tags: Each beat carries an `origin`. 'vetted' = it maps onto the gem-AGNOSTIC vocabulary in firehose.py (_MOVERS / _EARLY / _SECTORS / _CATALYSTS), which was deliberately scrubbed of gem sub-niches reverse-engineered from known winners. 'forward' = added later on the forward side, and its atoms sit closer to a specific gem's thesis (rare earth, DRAM, uranium). Tagged, not dropped: the forward runs these beats today, so the backtest must run them too or it stops being a proxy. The tag is here so the hindsight question stays auditable -- when reading a backtest number, check how much of it came through a 'forward'-origin beat.
_named_chokepoints_note: The chokepoint beat names Hormuz / Suez / Panama / Malacca / Bab el-Mandeb. These are the standard enumerated list of global maritime chokepoints in any trade-geography reference, NOT terms reverse-engineered from this repo's gems -- the alternative (the bare word 'war') was measured above as the single worst source of noise in the pool. Flagged here because one of them does coincide with the BWET tanker thesis.

gem_beats.query: under the radar small cap stock
export ban tariff sanctions stock beneficiary
uranium nuclear fuel supply squeeze stock
upcoming FDA election vote stock anticipation

coverage_beats.query: freight trucking rail air cargo logistics stocks
steel copper lithium aluminum titanium coal mining stocks
electric power grid pipeline energy infrastructure stocks
stock surges skyrockets all-time high record
best performing ETF little-known skyrocketing surging
gold silver miners ETF surging record high
power grid AI datacenter energy ETF surging

_spam_two_tier_note: SPLIT 2026-08-08 after an LLM audit of what the filter threw away (scripts/judge_dropped.py). A blind judge re-read 200 dropped headlines and confirmed 11 (5.5%) were real catalyst reporting -- 'NVIDIA Price Target Raised to $225 After $100B OpenAI Deal', 'Regeneron Scores FDA Approval, JP Morgan Reaffirms $800 Price Target', 'SQM Stock Gets $53 Price Target From BofA as Lithium Prices Rally'. Extrapolated, one over-broad regex was discarding ~240 real articles a year, and they are exactly the class this strategy exists to catch. spam_title_patterns = HARD: pure machine plumbing (13F churn, Form-4, listicles, transcripts, quote pages) that is never salvageable. spam_title_patterns_soft = an ANALYST ACTION or a TECHNICAL-SIGNAL template, which is boilerplate ONLY when it is the whole story -- a soft match is spared when the headline also names a catalyst (catalyst_exemption). Judge the filter by what it DROPS, not by whether the regex matches: testing a regex with a regex is circular, which is why the audit uses a model that is never told a filter was involved. The exemption vocabulary was widened twice against measured false positives (earnings/outlook, then agreement/divestiture/expansion/talks). It is inherently open-ended -- catalyst language is not enumerable -- so this was stopped at a measured ~3% residual rather than chased to zero, since every added term also admits more boilerplate. Extended 2026-08-08 from a strong-model FALSE-NEGATIVE audit of the CORPUS (not the drops): ~52% of surviving articles were judged noise, concentrated in template-shaped categories the original patterns never covered -- earnings previews, IPO lot-size/GMP pages, conference and webinar invitations, dividend declarations, technical-signal bots, volume rankings and 'Should You Buy X After Its N% Rally' listicles. Those went to the HARD tier because no catalyst redeems them; offerings and all-time-high templates went SOFT because a real deal can make them news. Two of those additions were reverted the same day after measurement: a '(what|why) you need to know$' rule was matching a Benzinga headline SUFFIX rather than a story type (883 real articles), and 'should you buy' was demoted to soft. Net lesson: a pattern must describe the STORY, never a publisher's house style -- and every pattern addition needs an FP re-measure, because this batch raised the spam stage's false-positive rate 2.7% -> 6.7% before correction. THE WHOLE 2026-08-08 junk batch was then REVERTED. Measured across three passes the spam stage's false-positive rate went 2.7% -> 6.7% -> 11.3% while the corpus junk rate did not measurably move (removing ~2.5k of 39k articles cannot shift a ~52% rate by more than ~3pp, which is inside the sampling error at n=300). The batch bought no measurable precision and cost real recall, so it is gone. Recorded so it is not re-attempted: the corpus's residual noise is NOT template-shaped enough for headline regex, and the scout -- which reads the whole pool and judges -- is the intended backstop for it. MEASURED 2026-08-10 and FIXED: `expands?` was removed from catalyst_exemption. It directly cancelled the soft pattern `short interest ... expands`, which exists to kill 'Short Interest in X Expands By 21.5%'. Of the 62 soft-matched survivors that term spared, 62 were short-interest boilerplate and ZERO were genuine catalysts -- so the deletion costs no recall. `expansion` is kept: it carries the capacity/capex sense that IS a catalyst.
_spam_pattern_note: A/B'd 2026-08-07 against domain-blocking. These domain-AGNOSTIC patterns remove the automated-filing headline CLASS (13F churn, Form-4 insider moves, 52-week-high bots, short-interest bots) wherever it appears, and they are correctly SURGICAL on real outlets -- insidermonkey.com kept 99% of its articles and financialcontent.com 100%, because those sites' boilerplate is a small minority of genuine reporting. What patterns CANNOT do is clear a site that is nothing BUT boilerplate: tickerreport / dailypolitical / themarketsdaily still had 66-72% of their articles survive, because the bots have unbounded template variants ('Sees Large Decline', 'Grows Position in', 'Stock Price Up 9.4%'). Those three are handled by mill_block instead. Patterns for the class, domain-block for the source -- each doing the job the other can't.
_english_only_note: engine.english_only maps to the SQL predicate `TranslationInfo IS NULL`, which keeps only English-ORIGIN articles (GDELT machine-translates foreign coverage and marks it here). It is the LARGEST single filter in the pipeline -- measured at 88.5M rows/year, 64.6% of everything GDELT indexes -- and until 2026-08-09 it was a bare condition in the SQL with no knob, no note, and no audit, so it never appeared in the funnel dashboard at all. Promoted to config because a scope decision of that size should be visible and switchable, not buried. Set false to admit foreign-origin coverage, e.g. to reach non-US press writing about US-listed ADRs -- but expect roughly 3x the rows and note that the beat keywords are English, so recall on translated text will be poor until they are too.
_org_stoplist_note: MATCHED ON WORD BOUNDARIES, not as substrings (src/gkg._stoplist_re). The substring form silently discarded real listed companies whose names merely CONTAIN a stop token: `sec` killed SecureWorks / Secure Energy Services / Second Sight Medical, `epa` killed EPAM Systems, `russell` killed Russell Metals. Fixed 2026-08-10. Note some entries ARE themselves listed companies (Nasdaq/NDAQ, Cboe/CBOE, MSCI, FactSet/FDS, Morningstar/MORN) -- they stay because they appear far more often as index/data providers than as subjects, but an article genuinely about one of them as a company is collateral damage. MEASURED 2026-08-10, and the reason the generic-institution tokens below exist: switching to word boundaries removed an ACCIDENT that was load-bearing -- `epa` had been matching 'd-EPA-rtment', which is what kept Defense Department / Department of Government Efficiency / state banking departments out of the pool. Without a replacement the fix readmitted 1,457 rows per 24 chunks of which 82% were government-only subjects, i.e. exactly the general news the org test exists to exclude. So `department`/`ministry`/`agency`/... are now EXPLICIT, and the index-sector artifacts ('Select Sector', 'Software Sector') with them. Lesson: before removing a filter that looks wrong, measure what it was actually catching.
